Structure as printed: Section A 14 marks = Q1 in three groups, (A) fill-in-the-blanks 4x1 [p08], (B) MCQ 7x1 [p08-p09], (C) passage 3x1 [p10]; Section B 20 marks = Q2-Q11 at 2 each [p12-p19]; Section C 21 marks = Q12-Q18 at 3 each [p20-p27]; Section D 15 marks = Q19-Q21 at 5 each [p28-p32]. Total 70. Question numbers run 1-21 unbroken; section totals checked against the printed section headings (14/20/21/15). Internal choices (bare OR line): Q9, Q16, Q21 only; each alternative is its own row with choice set. Q1 refs carry the group letter, 1(A)(i) ... 1(C)(iii), because the subpart numerals restart in each group. Every question was followed by a MARKING SCHEME block (21 of 21).

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.instruction: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.
rows.context: The rate of a reaction depends on the concentration of reactants. The rate law for a hypothetical reaction \(\mathrm{aA + bB \longrightarrow cC + dD}\) is rate \(= k\,[A]^x[B]^y\) where \(x\) and \(y\) are calculated experimentally and known as *order of reaction*. In most cases, the mechanism of a reaction is not straight forward but broken down in simple elementary steps. These steps represent the progress of overall reaction at the molecular level.
rows.text: What will be the order of reaction if the unit of \(k\) is \(\mathrm{mol^{-2}\,L^2\,s^{-1}}\)?

An organic compound [A] has molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\). When compound [A] is treated with \(\mathrm{SOCl_2}\), it yields compound [B]. On heating with \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), compound [B] forms compound [C]. Compound [C] forms compound [D] on reaction with \(\mathrm{Br_2/KOH}\). Compound [D] responds to carbylamine test.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.text:
In the reaction \(\mathrm{2NO + O_2 \longrightarrow 2NO_2}\), the rate law is rate \(= \mathrm{k[NO][O_2]^2}\).
(i) How will the rate of reaction change if [NO] concentration is doubled and \(\mathrm{[O_2]}\) concentration is halved at the same time?
(ii) Write the order of reaction if [NO] concentration is in large excess.

When an organic compound [A] having molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\) is treated with aqueous KOH, the rate of reaction depends on concentration of compound [A] only. But when compound [B], with the same molecular formula, reacts with aqueous KOH, the rate of reaction depends on the concentration of compound [B] as well as of KOH. Compound [B] is a structural isomer of compound [A].
Identify compounds [A] and [B].

Write a balanced chemical equation for each of the following:
(i) Ethyl cyanide is reduced with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\).
(ii) Aniline is treated with bromine water.

The scientist van't Hoff introduced a factor \((i)\) to account for the extent of association or dissociation of solutes. It is mathematically expressed as:
\(i = \dfrac{\text{normal molecular mass}}{\text{experimental molecular mass}}\)
In case of association, \(i < 1\) and in case of dissociation \(i > 1\).
(i) In the calculation of molecular mass of \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) by using a colligative property, what will be the value of van't Hoff factor if the solute is 25% dissociated?
(ii) Find the value of van't Hoff factor for a dilute aqueous solution of benzoic acid in water when it is completely associated to form a dimer.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.text:
Osmotic pressure is the external pressure which should be applied to stop the flow of solvent into the solution when the two are separated by a semipermeable membrane. The osmotic pressure is a colligative property. Two solutions having the same osmotic pressure are called *isotonic*. If there are two solutions and one of them is of lower osmotic pressure, it is called *hypotonic* while the other is called *hypertonic*.
Answer the questions given below.
(a) What will happen if red blood corpuscles are placed in a 5% NaCl solution which is a hypertonic solution?
(b) Show that osmotic pressure \((\pi)\) is a colligative property.
(c) Calculate the amount of pressure required to stop osmosis of a solution when 40 g of \(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}\) is added to 1 L of water at 298 K.
(Given: Na = 23, O = 16, S = 32 and R = \(0{\cdot}0821\) L atm \(\mathrm{K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\))
(d) Briefly discuss the process of *reverse osmosis* followed to desalinate sea water and convert it into drinking water.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.text:
(a) An aqueous solution is made by dissolving 10 g of glucose \(\mathrm{(C_6H_{12}O_6)}\) in 90 g of water at 300 K. If the vapour pressure of pure water at 300 K is \(32{\cdot}8\) mm Hg, what would be the vapour pressure of the solution?
(Given: C = 12, H = 1 and O = 16)
(b) A solution containing \(12{\cdot}5\) g of a non-electrolyte solute in 175 g of water gave boiling point of \(100{\cdot}70^\circ\)C. Calculate the molecular mass of the solute.
(Given: \(K_b\) for water = \(0{\cdot}52\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
(c) Why are soda water bottles sealed under high pressure?
rows._flag: (c) is Henry's law (Solubility); (a)-(b) carry the bulk, filed under Colligative Properties.
